title: Phosphorylate and Spare Not
body_text: Now here’s a biochemical weapon I hadn’t seen before. This recent paper reports a technique used by a particular bacteriophage (T7) against its bacterial targets. One of the proteins it codes for is a kinase (T7K) whose functions have not been well understood. You can say that again! These authors report that T7K actually is the most promiscuous kinase ever characterized, and it phosphorylates nearly all the host proteins it encounters (!) The kinase especially likes DNA-binding domains of its target proteins, and phosphorylation is well known to disrupt those functions. It certainly should - such DNABDs are ready to attract to DNA with its inescapable phosphate backbone, so sticking such a negatively charged phosphate itself into them leads to a severe mismatch and decreases in binding affinity and function. Testing across a range of E. coli types, the authors find that this kinase activity disrupts a whole list of host defense systems, as well it might. And there’s a neat shutoff system at work, too. It appears that although it’s capable of phosphorylating most anything (including its own phage protein brethren), the main functions seem to be disruption of those DNA-binding regions. This occurs in a huge burst of activity (several minutes worth) which stops as the T7K protein phosphorylates itself. The paper includes a search for homologs of this blunderbuss, which turn out to be almost exclusively in other bacteriophages. The hypothesis is that the mechanism these kinases use is something you can get away with in a bacteriophage, but perhaps not in any higher organism that has a need to be more discriminating about what gets phosphorylated and when. Evolutionarily it’ll be interesting to see if later kinases evolved from this sort of take-no-prisoners class, or if there are separate paths involved. And as usual for these sorts of discoveries, keep in mind that until this time we had no idea that this was happening. What else is out there right now that we have no idea about?
